paras: The Double Horn Mob attack on the Fall Creek camp meeting was the breaking up of a Methodist campmeeting on Fall creek, Texas, by about twenty men calling themselves the "Double Horn Mob" in late July 1881. The men cut saddles and stake ropes, threw rocks, fired pistols and beat a Black man who was asleep in a wagon on the grounds. An Austin Statesman correspondent reported it as a fresh "outrage" and urged that the men, several said to be known, be punished.

The Fall creek campmeeting was an annual gathering, conducted that year by the Southern Methodist Church and attended by other denominations. The correspondent, writing from Cypress Mill in Blanco County, placed the attack in a run of "outrage" cases in Bell and Burnet counties, including whippings and the lynching of Bell County prisoners. He did not name the county of the campgrounds, though he treated the episode as Burnet County's.

The correspondent could find no reason for the attack; the "impression" was that the men were drunk and armed. They cut the saddles and stake ropes of those attending, threw rocks at people who came out, shot off pistols, and cursed and mimicked the preachers, until the meeting was broken up. Among their acts, they beat "a negro who was sleeping in a wagon on the campgrounds"; the man was not named and the extent of his injuries was not reported.

According to the correspondent's informants, several of the men were known, and they expected the sheriff of Burnet County, whom they called "a terror when he goes on the war-path," to pursue them. No report of arrests, charges or a trial appears in the coverage found.

The only report found is a letter dated July 28 under the heading "From Blanco County" in the Weekly Democratic Statesman of Austin on August 4, 1881. The writer called the attackers a "self-styled mob," "villains" and "bloods" and urged their punishment for disturbing religious worship and destroying property. His indignation centered on the cutting of a young lady's saddle, while the beating of the Black man appeared as one item in a list of the mob's acts.
